headline: September inflation came in hot at 3.7% on a 9.1% jump in gasoline, the 10 year yield jumped to about 5.28%, and banks split again: Morgan Stanley confirmed the trading boom while Bank of America missed and took a $1.2 billion penalty.
summary: September CPI rose 0.6% in the month and 3.7% from a year ago, above the 3.6% forecast and up from 3.4%. Energy did most of it: gasoline rose 9.1% and the energy index 5.2%, while core prices rose 0.3% and 2.6% a year, a touch above the 0.2% and 2.5% expected. The 10 year yield rose more than 6 basis points to about 5.28% and stock futures turned lower, with the Nasdaq 100 down about 0.5% before the open. Morgan Stanley beat on a 41% jump in equities trading, which confirms Goldman's boom, but Bank of America missed on weaker trading plus a $1.2 billion regulatory charge and fell about 7% premarket; BlackRock hit a record $15.5 trillion in assets. Overnight a Houthi missile hit Aramco's headquarters building in Dhahran and Brent rose to about $106.30, while ASML beat and said demand will outrun its supply into 2028, yet memory kept sliding, with the KOSPI down for a sixth day. The dashboard's first finished grade is a miss: the ANET swing from Oct 6 hit its stop for a 1R loss. Setups still show Oct 12 closes, no setup is near a volume confirmed breakout, and TSMC reports Thursday.

regime.why: Inflation is heating up from oil, not from everything: core is 2.6% while headline is 3.7%. But the bond market does not care why, and a 5.28% 10 year squeezes stock values, especially crowded AI hardware. Trading desks and exchanges are winning from the volatility. Keep normal size only on breakouts that close over the pivot on 1.5x volume, and wait for TSMC Thursday before adding chip exposure.

signals.title: September CPI runs hot at 3.7% on gasoline, core stays at 2.6%, and the 10 year jumps to about 5.28%
signals.what_happened: The consumer price index rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% from a year earlier, above the 3.6% Dow Jones forecast and up from 3.4% in August (CNBC, CBS). Core prices, without food and energy, rose 0.3% in the month and 2.6% a year, against 0.2% and 2.5% expected. The energy index jumped 5.2% and gasoline 9.1%, about half of the headline gain; shelter rose 0.4% and food was flat. After the release the 10 year yield rose more than 6 basis points to 5.278% and the 30 year to 5.59%, both near last week's 24 year highs. S&P 500 futures fell about 0.2% to 0.3%, Nasdaq 100 futures about 0.5% and Dow futures 62 points; WTI was up nearly 2% near $96.
signals.so_what: This is an oil shock showing up in prices, not a broad wage and rent spiral: core at 2.6% is tame. Who pays: drivers, airlines, and anyone holding long bonds. Who gets paid: oil producers and refiners now, and banks' trading desks from the swings. Second order: the Fed meets Oct 28 with headline inflation rising for a second month, so a cut is off the table and markets will keep pricing risk of a hike; that keeps long rates high and pressures the most expensive growth stocks. Third order: high yields plus high oil is the mix that cracked crowded trades in 2022. What would make this wrong: oil falls on a Hormuz reopening or a real Russia Ukraine energy deal, and October gasoline gives back September's jump.
signals.for_you: Swing: rates up and futures down means no breakout is likely to confirm at the open; XOM and COP benefit from the oil story but still need 20.4M+ and 10M+ shares. Puts: higher rates make put premiums a bit richer, but only sell on names you want to own; PFE $27 and C $122 stay (see Setups for live quotes). Long term: no change to buy zones today; be slow with high valuation tech while the 10 year is above 5.25%.

signals.title: Banks, day two: Morgan Stanley confirms the equities boom, Bank of America misses with a $1.2 billion penalty, BlackRock hits $15.5 trillion
signals.since_yesterday: Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and BlackRock reported on Oct 14: MS equities trading rose about 41% and BAC missed with a $1.2 billion regulatory charge.
signals.what_happened: Morgan Stanley earned $3.03 a share against $2.91 expected (LSEG) on revenue of $20.34 billion against $19.95 billion. Equities trading rose about 41% to $5.8 billion, about $909 million above estimates, helped by Asia; fixed income trading fell about 7% to $2.01 billion and investment banking rose 2% but missed (CNBC). Bank of America earned $0.91 a share, or $1.08 adjusted, against $1.10 expected, after a $1.2 billion non deductible settlement over anti money laundering and sanctions failures (OCC and FinCEN). Revenue of about $30.1 billion missed by about $570 million, mostly in trading, while net interest income rose 8% to $16.4 billion; the stock was down about 7% premarket. BlackRock's assets reached $15.5 trillion at Sep 30 (8-K), with about $205 billion of net inflows in the quarter and adjusted EPS of $15.93 against about $13.97 expected.
signals.so_what: Yesterday's question was whether JPMorgan's cost squeeze is broad. BAC says partly: its miss is a one time penalty and soft trading, not runaway costs, and its lending income grew 8%. MS answers the other question: yes, the equities trading boom is shared, but fixed income is weak at MS. The money is flowing to whoever earns from volume and volatility (MS, GS, exchanges) and to the biggest asset gatherer (BLK), not to plain lenders. Third order: record flows into ETFs keep feeding index buying of the largest stocks. What would make this wrong: a calmer market in Q4 would shrink the trading windfall fast.
signals.for_you: Long term: CBOE is Buy zone now and is the cleanest way the dashboard plays the trading boom. BLK is Buy zone, wait for the chart: its up/down volume is 0.89 and needs to get back over 1.0; record inflows could do that. BAC and MS have no dashboard verdict. Puts: C $122 stays, but let banks settle a day after BAC's drop. Swing: no bank is a setup.

signals.title: ASML beats and says demand will outrun supply into 2028, but memory keeps sliding: Micron down 3.6%, KOSPI down a sixth day
signals.since_yesterday: ASML beat and raised on Oct 14, but Micron fell another 3.62% on Oct 13 and the KOSPI's Oct 14 bounce failed.
signals.what_happened: ASML reported Q3 sales of EUR 11.7 billion and net income of EUR 5.0 billion against about EUR 4.13 billion expected, with a 57.5% gross margin. It guided Q4 sales to EUR 14.2 to 15.2 billion, raised 2026 to EUR 44 to 45 billion, its third raise this year, and CEO Fouquet said planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet demand. The ADR was up about 1.6% premarket. Memory did not follow: Micron closed down 3.62% at $953.19 on Oct 13 after Netlist filed patent complaints at the ITC and workers at its Taoyuan site voted to authorize a strike. Correcting yesterday: the KOSPI closed Oct 13 at 6,035.35, down 5.46% (it broke 6,000 only intraday), with SK hynix down 10.09%. On Oct 14 an early 2% bounce faded and it closed down 0.44% at 6,008.81. Separately, Microsoft unveiled its Maia 300 inference chip on Oct 12, built by TSMC for 2027 volume; Evercore estimates Maia at about 10% of Microsoft's AI chip spend by early 2027.
signals.so_what: The tool maker with the monopoly says the build out is still supply limited, which is the opposite of a capex pause. So the selling in memory is about who captures the profit, not whether AI spending continues. Who pays: memory makers if China adds supply. Who gets paid: the chokepoints that every chip needs (ASML, TSMC). Custom chips like Maia also send more work to TSMC, not less. What would make this wrong: TSMC on Thursday guides Q4 or 2027 capex below expectations, or says customers are pushing out orders.
signals.for_you: Swing: still no memory or chip equipment swings; ANET (entry 217.85, needs 8.7M+ shares, up/down 1.44) waits for TSMC. Long term: LRCX is Buy zone now but sits in the memory selloff, so wait for Thursday. TSM and ASML have no buy zone verdict (Not enough data). Thursday 2am ET: TSMC margins against the 65% to 67% guide and 2027 capex are the tell.

signals.title: Houthis hit Aramco's headquarters, more ships struck near Hormuz, and Ukraine's refinery pause holds a third day
signals.since_yesterday: A Houthi missile hit an Aramco building in Dhahran on Oct 14, and UKMTO reported a tanker and two container ships hit near Hormuz on Oct 13.
signals.what_happened: A Houthi ballistic missile hit an Aramco administrative building at its Dhahran headquarters early Oct 14, causing a limited fire and damaging the top floors used by executives, reportedly including the CEO's office (AP). AP's officials reported no casualties; IBTimes, citing Riyadh, said four were hurt. A Houthi official said Russia and China have reached out about a ceasefire. On Oct 13 UKMTO reported a tanker struck in the Strait of Hormuz (Iran said it hit a mine) and two container ships hit by projectiles. Brent settled just under $106 on Oct 13 (Bloomberg) and was up 0.58% at $106.30 by 8:03am ET, with WTI up 1.57% at $95.62. In Europe, no Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were reported through Oct 13, but Russia keeps hitting Ukraine's grid, and the US eased sanctions on Russian diesel just before the 'energy ceasefire' was announced.
signals.so_what: The war has moved from shipping lanes to the headquarters of the world's biggest oil company. Physical damage to output is not reported, so this is a risk premium, not lost barrels. Who gets paid: US producers with no Gulf exposure (XOM, COP, CVX) and US LNG exporters. Who pays: airlines and every consumer, which feeds straight into the CPI story above. The Russia and China ceasefire outreach is the swing factor: a real Houthi truce would take a few dollars off Brent quickly. More Russian diesel on the market is why diesel is easing even as crude stays high.
signals.for_you: Swing: XOM closed 172.15 on Oct 12, 0.4% under its 172.91 pivot, with up/down 1.22 (accumulation), but needs 20.4M+ shares on the breakout day; a news gap on light volume is weak, wait for the close. COP: entry 141.91, needs 10M+ shares, up/down 1.12. CVX: entry 218.23, needs 12.8M+ shares, up/down only 1.00. All three report Oct 30 or Nov 5, so a swing has two weeks before earnings. Puts: no energy put idea.

signals.title: Health follow up: UnitedHealth's gap did not hold, and Medtronic's MiniMed swap closes with 18.3% proration
signals.since_yesterday: UNH closed down 0.2% at $377.76 on Oct 13 after being up over 4%, and Medtronic set the final proration at 18.289133% on Oct 14.
signals.what_happened: UnitedHealth was up more than 4% early on Oct 13 after its beat and raise, but it gave it all back and closed down 0.2% at $377.76 (WSJ recap, StockAnalysis). J&J was down about 2.9% premarket after its beat; its close was not found. Medtronic's MiniMed exchange offer closed oversubscribed: 297.5 million Medtronic shares were tendered, it accepted 55,032,401 at the capped ratio of 4.5939 MiniMed shares each, and the final proration factor is 18.289133%. Medtronic gave up its whole remaining MiniMed stake of 252.8 million shares.
signals.so_what: UNH shows the market still doubts the insurer recovery: a big beat sold into is a sign that holders are using good news to get out. For Medtronic the deal works like a large buyback paid in MiniMed stock: 55 million shares is about 4.3% of its roughly 1.28 billion shares (dashboard fundamentals), so future earnings per share rise without spending cash. Tendered shares that were not accepted go back to holders now, which can add a little selling pressure for a few days. What would make this wrong: MiniMed trades poorly and the market blames Medtronic for the spin.
signals.for_you: Puts: UNH and JNJ were on your MT Put Candidates list this week, but the UNH gap failed and its up/down volume is 0.78, so no put on it yet; JNJ is rated Wait (58% over fair value). Long term: MDT is Buy zone now (zone 84.33 to 92.36, Oct 12 close 91.93 near the top), so a first tranche fits and more if it dips toward the middle of the zone.

cycle.quadrant_why: Inflation: September CPI rose to 3.7% from 3.4%, the second rise in a row, driven by a 9.1% jump in gasoline; core is only 2.6%. Growth: banks report rising lending income (BAC net interest income up 8%, JPMorgan up 13%) and booming trading, and loss provisions are falling. In Dalio's four seasons this is still rising inflation with steady growth, now confirmed by the data.
cycle.short_term_debt_cycle: Late, with tightening pressure rising. The Fed is at 3.75% to 4.00% and meets Oct 28 with headline inflation going the wrong way. The 10 year jumped to about 5.28% on the print, near its 24 year high of about 5.36% on Oct 7. Late cycle stress shows first in the most crowded, most foreign owned trades, which is where the selling is: Korean and US memory chips.
cycle.long_term_debt_cycle: Late. Debt is high and long rates are above 5%. When inflation is driven by an oil shock, the central bank cannot cut to help growth without risking more inflation, which is the squeeze Dalio describes late in the long term cycle.
cycle.big_cycle: Four of the five forces are active. Debt and money: 5.28% long rates and 3.7% inflation. Internal order: a split US three weeks before the Nov 3 midterms. External order: the Gulf war has reached Aramco's headquarters, and Russia keeps striking Ukraine's grid during a one sided energy pause. Technology: ASML says AI demand outruns its supply into 2028, the main tailwind.
tailwinds: ASML says AI chip tool demand will outrun supply through 2028.
Trading desks and asset gatherers are earning record fees (MS equities +41%, BlackRock at $15.5 trillion).
headwinds: Headline inflation at 3.7% and rising on oil.
A 10 year yield near 5.28%, close to a 24 year high.
War risk now hitting Saudi oil infrastructure and Hormuz shipping.

history.what: August 2022 CPI came in at 8.3% against 8.1% expected, with core up 0.6% in the month. The S&P 500 fell about 4.3% that day, its worst day since June 2020, and the Nasdaq fell 5.16%.
history.lesson: Markets punish surprises in core inflation hardest, because core tells the Fed whether inflation is spreading.

source.title: Dow tumbles 1,200 points for worst day since June 2020 after hot inflation report (NBC News, Sep 13, 2022)

history.what: Oil quadrupled and inflation surged. The S&P 500 fell about 48% from its January 1973 high to the October 1974 low, and even Exxon and Chevron fell about 44%.
history.lesson: In a true oil shock with rising inflation, almost nothing is safe. Cash and short duration held up best.

source.title: Museum of American Finance: 1970s Bear Market

history.what: The S&P 500 lost about 19% for the year while the energy sector returned more than 60%, the best sector by far.
history.lesson: In the rising inflation season, energy and real assets lead and long duration growth lags.

source.title: Investing Daily: The Leaders and Laggards of 2022

cycle.differences: Sep 2022 replaces the 2018 memory top today because today's setup is a CPI surprise, not a chip cycle. What is different: in 2022 core was rising 0.6% a month; today it rose 0.3% and the surprise is almost all gasoline, which is why futures fell only about 0.2% to 0.5%, not 4%. What is the same: long yields react first, and the most expensive growth stocks take the hit. If core starts to rise too, the 2022 playbook applies in full.
cycle.for_you: Swing: favor setups that benefit from oil and confirm on volume (XOM, COP), and skip chips until after TSMC. Puts: sell only where you would own the stock through a 20% drop; PFE $27 and C $122 still fit, energy and chips do not. Long term: buy quality in tranches, and treat high valuation tech as watch only while the 10 year is above 5.25%.

principle.text: Don't confuse what you wish were true with what is really true.
principle.applied: It is tempting to call this CPI 'just gasoline' and buy the dip in growth stocks. The truth is the bond market moved anyway: the 10 year rose about 6 basis points in minutes. Trade what yields and volume are doing, not what you hope the Fed will think.
